extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners working on federated learning, ML security/privacy, and fairness
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for robustness, privacy, and fairness in federated learning systems, including attack/defense models, non-malicious failure modes, and measures for fairness with and without sensitive attributes. Emphasizes practical constraints of cross-device deployments and open research directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global/per-client accuracy insufficient for backdoor detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Even metrics such as global training accuracy or per client training accuracy may not be enough to detect the presence of a backdoor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detection of backdoors requires metrics beyond simple accuracy measures; practitioners should use specialized backdoor detection techniques and not rely solely on aggregate accuracy statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between model update poisoning and data poisoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Data poisoning attacks are special cases of model update poisoning since they alter client outputs; however, it is unclear which model update poisoning attacks can be achieved or approximated by data poisoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify the gap between attack types empirically (compare attack performance) and theoretically (dependence on number of corrupted clients, function class, model overparameterization). Use machine teaching and optimal-poisoning analyses where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness measured by performance on white-box adversarial examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Robustness is often measured by the model performance on white-box adversarial examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should include white-box attacks (strongest), and consider black-box and substitute-model attacks as well; be aware that robustness to one attack class may not generalize to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adversarial training provides some robustness but is attack-specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversarial training generally provides some robustness to white-box evasion attacks, but typically only to the specific type of adversarial examples incorporated during training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating adversarial training, test against a diverse set of perturbation types and consider that hyperparameters and formulation choices affect robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical constraints for adversarial training in federated settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapting adversarial training to federated learning is challenging because it may require many epochs, assumes IID data, requires setting perturbation bounds without inspecting client data, and is computationally expensive for clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of adversarial defenses for federated learning must account for limited local data exposures, non-IID distributions, client compute/memory/power constraints, and difficulty of choosing perturbation norms; develop on-device robust optimization techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity of adversarial training to minimax formulation and hyperparameters
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no canonical formulation of adversarial training; choices such as the minimax optimization problem and hyperparameters (e.g., learning rate) can significantly affect model robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and analyze optimization choices when reporting robustness results; include ablations over hyperparameters and formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defending model update poisoning using differential privacy (clipping + aggregate + noise)
rubrics_metrics.description: The service provider can bound the contribution of any individual client by (1) enforcing a norm constraint on the client model update (e.g., by clipping the client updates), (2) aggregating the clipped updates, (3) and adding Gaussian noise to the aggregate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach prevents overfitting to individual updates and mirrors DP training; evaluate effectiveness against targeted attacks and extend experiments to more general adversarial scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: DP hyperparameter selection must consider model and adversary characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unclear how hyperparameters for DP (such as the size of L2 norm bounds and noise variance) can be chosen as a function of the model size and architecture, as well as the fraction of malicious devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperparameter selection for DP should be studied empirically and theoretically with respect to model architecture, scale, and assumed adversary strength (number/fraction of compromised clients).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential privacy trade-offs when defending against data poisoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Differential privacy can improve robustness to data poisoning by limiting the influence of a few training examples, but it requires injecting noise which can hurt model performance and assumes the adversary controls few devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating DP defenses against poisoning, measure the performance cost of noise and the adversary model (how many examples/devices they control). Consider group-privacy degradation as number of attacked points increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: DP-based defenses for inference-time attacks and their drawbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Making the predictor itself differentially private randomizes predictions (undesirable for interpretability), though alternatives add noise and then release the prediction with highest probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess utility and interpretability trade-offs when applying DP at prediction time; consider more sophisticated mechanisms that preserve deterministic-like outputs while providing privacy guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client reporting failure considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Clients may fail during model broadcast, local computation, or reporting; stragglers or dropouts can reduce participating clients and complicate secure aggregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations include selecting more devices per round, improving SecAgg efficiency, designing asynchronous SecAgg protocols, or aggregating over multiple rounds to include stragglers; evaluate effect on convergence and failure probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data pipeline failure detection under privacy constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Bugs or unintended actions in local preprocessing pipelines (e.g., inverting pixels, concatenating words) can drastically alter training, but are hard to detect due to federated data restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop debugging methods that do not inspect raw data (e.g., train DP generative models to synthesize data for pipeline debugging) and evaluate their ability to reveal common preprocessing errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noisy model updates as a non-malicious failure mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Model updates may be distorted due to network, architectural factors, or noisy client data (noisy features/labels), harming convergence similarly to mild poisoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess robustness of federated training algorithms (e.g., federated averaging) to varying levels and types of noise; develop computationally-light defenses appropriate for resource-constrained clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between secure aggregation (SecAgg) and robustness techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: SecAgg ensures servers only see an aggregate (protecting privacy) but makes many defenses harder since individual updates are hidden; compatibility with non-linear Byzantine-robust aggregators is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing defenses, consider whether they require individual updates; explore ways to make robust aggregators compatible with SecAgg or design privacy-preserving verification like range proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for computation- and communication-efficient range proofs under SecAgg
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing approaches (e.g., Bulletproofs) can guarantee DP-based clipping is compatible with SecAgg, but computation- and communication-efficient range proofs are still needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate privacy-preserving proof mechanisms in federated settings for overheads and scalability; ensure they enable necessary checks (e.g., clipping bounds) without violating privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual fairness definition
rubrics_metrics.description: If people with similar characteristics receive quite different outcomes, then this violates the criterion of individual fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure similarity of individuals and check outcome consistency; in federated contexts, devise privacy-preserving similarity metrics or proxies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic fairness definition (group-based metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: If certain sensitive groups receive different patterns of outcomes—such as different false negative rates—this can violate criteria of demographic fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate group-wise metrics (e.g., false positive/negative rates, calibration) across sensitive groups where possible; account for sampling/representation biases inherent to federated selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfactual fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterfactual fairness requires that a user receive the same treatment as they would have if they had been a member of a different group, after taking all causally relevant pathways into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply causal analysis where feasible; recognize practical difficulty in federated settings where causally-relevant data and sensitive attributes may be unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Device-selection/time-of-day bias
rubrics_metrics.description: If devices are selected for updates when plugged-in or fully charged, then model updates/evaluations computed at different times of day may correlate with day/night schedules, introducing bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor and correct for time-of-day selection biases in participation; consider stratified sampling or weighting to mitigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-representation of devices connected during low-connection times
rubrics_metrics.description: If devices are selected among eligible devices at a given time, devices connected at times when few devices are connected may be over-represented in aggregated output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze participation distributions over time; design selection protocols to avoid over-weighting atypical connection-time populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias due to preferential retention of faster device outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: If selected devices are more likely to have their output kept when output is computed faster, outputs from devices with faster processors may be over-represented (correlated with socioeconomic status), and devices with less data may be over-represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid selection/retention policies that favor faster processors; consider fairness-aware sampling or normalization by device capacity/data volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unequal data amounts across nodes causing representation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: If data nodes have different amounts of data, federated learning may weigh contributions from heavy users more, disadvantaging under-represented populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aggregation weighting schemes or per-device regularization to counteract unequal influence from heavy-data nodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic/latency-driven under-representation
rubrics_metrics.description: If update frequency depends on latency, geographic regions and populations with slower devices or networks may be under-represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design participation and aggregation protocols robust to latency differences; consider compensatory sampling or weighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socioeconomic under-representation due to device ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: If potential users do not own devices for socio-economic reasons, they may be under- or un-represented in training and evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, measure and account for coverage gaps; be cautious when generalizing model performance to underrepresented populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unweighted aggregation can disadvantage certain devices/populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Unweighted aggregation of model loss across selected devices during federated training may disadvantage model performance on certain devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate per-device performance and consider weighted aggregation or fairness-aware objectives to ensure equitable performance distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias from data-generating processes and product design
rubrics_metrics.description: Training data derived from user interactions with products that lack inclusive design may reflect coping strategies and result in models that ignore or perpetuate poor experiences for some groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate upstream product design issues, and when learning from interaction data, attempt to detect and correct such biases rather than only adjusting model post-hoc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for methods to identify/correct bias and post-hoc fairness corrections in federated settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited prior research exists on identifying and correcting bias in federated settings; methods for applying post-hoc fairness corrections are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and evaluate privacy-preserving bias-detection and correction methods (e.g., adversarial methods, DP-aware adjustments) and report limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness without access to sensitive attributes (DRO and multicalibration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaches like distributionally-robust optimization (DRO) and multicalibration optimize for worst-case or calibrated outcomes across subsets without explicit sensitive attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess scalability of DRO/multicalibration to federated, high-dimensional data; evaluate whether these methods achieve equitable performance across unknown subgroups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reframing fairness as equal access to effective models
rubrics_metrics.description: When sensitive attributes are unavailable, fairness might be reframed as equal access to effective models—maximizing model utility across all individuals regardless of demographic identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personalization and per-device performance metrics to operationalize this conception; measure distribution of model utility over users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization as a fairness mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalization can be used to improve fairness by tailoring models to device- or user-specific distributions, potentially equalizing performance across individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate personalization approaches for both utility and fairness tradeoffs; ensure personalization does not exacerbate privacy risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling challenges for DRO/multicalibration in federated learning
rubrics_metrics.description: DRO and multicalibration pose scaling challenges with large n (number of users) and p (feature dimensionality) which have not yet been addressed in federated contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing DRO/multicalibration solutions, include analysis and experiments on computational and communication feasibility at federation scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-offs between differential privacy and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentially-private learning can have disparate impact on sensitive subgroups and may obscure group membership necessary to measure fairness, creating tension between privacy and fairness objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate empirical disparate impacts of DP, consider hybrid approaches (some users donate lesser privacy), and explore adaptive DP mechanisms that preserve minority subgroup performance by modifying noise/clipping per-group representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating fairness impacts when sensitive attributes are unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: It is difficult to identify subgroups and quantify the 'price' of differential privacy on fairness when sensitive attributes are not available in federated settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop proxy measurements, unsupervised subgroup discovery, or attribute-independent fairness metrics and quantify uncertainty in fairness assessments due to missing attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leveraging federation to improve dataset diversity and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Federated learning enables decentralized training across previously siloed datasets (e.g., across institutions), offering opportunities to improve model diversity and fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically and theoretically evaluate how cross-institution federation affects diversity, fairness, privacy, and performance; measure whether increased diversity yields fairness gains and how DP mechanisms modulate those gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated evaluation of robustness, privacy, and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: An important open challenge is to develop a joint understanding and integrated evaluation of federated learning systems that are robust, private, and fair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design benchmarks and experiments that measure interactions and trade-offs among robustness (poisoning/evasion), differential privacy, and fairness, not just isolated properties.
